cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Superstition – (noun) excessively credulous belief in and reverence for supernatural causality.

p.em: Example: Sam suffers from continuous bad luck until a black cat drops a lucky penny.

cosy-blockquote.p: Fortunate – (adjective) favored by or involving good luck; lucky.

p.em: Example: The inhabitants of the Land of Luck enjoy a perfectly fortunate existence.

cosy-blockquote.p: Coincidence – (noun) a remarkable concurrence of events or circumstances without apparent causal connection.

p.em: Example: Meeting Bob the talking cat seems like a wild coincidence, but it leads Sam to a new world.

cosy-blockquote.p: Harmony – (noun) a pleasing arrangement or combination of components.

p.em: Example: Sam learns that good luck and bad luck must coexist in delicate harmony.

cosy-blockquote.p: Foster care – (noun) a system in which a minor is placed into a ward, group home, or private home of a state-certified caregiver.

p.em: Example: Sam turns eighteen and leaves foster care, hoping to help little Hazel find a forever family.

cosy-blockquote.p: Resilience – (noun) the capacity to recover quickly from difficulties; toughness.

p.em: Example: Dealing with lifelong bad luck gives Sam incredible problem-solving resilience.

cosy-blockquote.p: Leprechaun – (noun) a mischievous elf in Irish folklore.

p.em: Example: Gerry the leprechaun manages security and lucky penny distribution in the upper realm.

cosy-blockquote.p: Unfortunate – (adjective) not blessed with good fortune; unlucky.

p.em: Example: Sam considers herself the most unfortunate girl in the world until she meets Bob.

cosy-blockquote.p: Equilibrium – (noun) a state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced.

p.em: Example: Destroying all bad luck disrupts the global equilibrium of human emotional growth.

cosy-blockquote.p: Belonging – (noun) an affinity for a place or situation; acceptance as a natural member.

p.em: Example: Sam's ultimate wish is not personal wealth, but finding a true sense of family belonging.

cosy-blockquote.p: Land of Luck – (noun) the hidden realm where good fortune is manufactured.

p.em: Example: Pristine emerald machinery works non-stop inside the Land of Luck.

cosy-blockquote.p: Land of Bad Luck – (noun) the cozy subterranean world where unluckiness is created.

p.em: Example: The Land of Bad Luck features warm, chaotic, rustic spaces filled with friendly creatures.

cosy-blockquote.p: Lucky penny – (noun) a magical coin that grants continuous good fortune.

p.em: Example: Sam desperately tries to secure a lucky penny so little Hazel can be adopted.

cosy-blockquote.p: Bob the cat – (noun) a clever Scottish black cat who secretly travels between realms.

p.em: Example: Bob pretends to be a normal stray cat until he accidentally speaks in front of Sam.

cosy-blockquote.p: Babe the Dragon – (noun) the elegant CEO dragon who scent-tests good luck dust.

p.em: Example: Babe the Dragon oversees the production of good luck with regal authority.

cosy-blockquote.p: Bad luck hazard – (noun) dark purple soot that causes instant minor mishaps.

p.em: Example: Spilling bad luck hazard causes doors to jam and items to drop immediately.

cosy-blockquote.p: Jinxed life – (noun) a lifestyle plagued by relentless minor accidents.

p.em: Example: Sam handles her jinxed life with humor and endless patience.

cosy-blockquote.p: Good vibes – (noun) positive social energy and optimism.

p.em: Example: The leprechauns maintain high spirits and good vibes to keep the luck factory running.

cosy-blockquote.p: Four-leaf clover – (noun) a rare clover variation symbolizing luck.

p.em: Example: Four-leaf clovers power the central engine of the lucky realm.

cosy-blockquote.p: Hazel – (noun) the young girl in foster care whom Sam loves like a sister.

p.em: Example: Sam prioritizes Hazel's happiness above all her own personal comfort.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Sam Greenfield has spent her whole life enduring hilarious, constant bad luck : from locked doors to flying breakfast toast. How does her positive attitude keep her going?
★ How do you maintain optimism when minor everyday obstacles seem to pile up against you?

When Sam ages out of foster care, her biggest goal is securing a lucky penny for little Hazel so Hazel can find an adoptive family. What does this show about her selflessness?
★ Why do people who have experienced personal hardship often feel driven to help others?

Bob the black cat loses his lucky penny and must return to the Land of Luck to avoid exile. How does Sam's accidental trip into his world change both their lives?
★ How can an unexpected mistake lead you into an exciting new opportunity or friendship?

Inside the Land of Luck, leprechauns, dragons, and pigs work together in an automated emerald factory. What does this magical bureaucracy reveal about luck?
★ Why do humans love coming up with logical explanations for random good or bad fortune?

Sam tries to navigate the Land of Luck while wearing a oversized leprechaun disguise. How does her natural bad luck disrupt their delicate machinery?
★ Have you ever tried to blend into a new environment where you felt completely out of place?

Babe the Dragon believes that bad luck is purely toxic and must be kept far away from society. How does her extreme perspective create imbalance?
★ Why is trying to eliminate all negative experiences from life unrealistic and unhelpful?

When Sam and Bob accidentally shut down both luck machines, they travel to the Land of Bad Luck below. How does the cozy atmosphere of Bad Luck surprise them?
★ Why do cozy, imperfect environments often feel warmer and more welcoming than flawless ones?

Root the goblin explains that bad luck teaches people resourcefulness, empathy, and humor. Do you agree with his philosophy on adversity?
★ What is a valuable lesson or skill you learned from dealing with an unlucky setback?

Sam realizes that Hazel doesn't need a magical lucky penny to be adopted : she needs loving parents who appreciate her as she is. How does this realization shift her focus?
★ Why are real emotional connections more reliable than superstitions or lucky charms?

Bob decides to stay in the human world with Sam and Hazel, choosing family over perfect good luck. What makes his choice a true happy ending?
★ How would you define a truly 'fortunate' life : having constant success or having people who love you?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: collaborative task or visual analysis in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, work together on the following task:

cosy-blockquote.p: Collaborative task or visual study.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: 1-on-1 guided visual description and task response with teacher.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Look at the prompt and discuss your response with your teacher:

cosy-blockquote.p: Collaborative task or visual study.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Director Peggy Holmes designed two contrasting realms: the sleek, shiny Land of Luck and the warm, rustic Land of Bad Luck. How does color palette build worldbuilding?
★ How does contrasting visual environments help communicate underlying themes in animated cinema?

Eva Noblezada provides the voice of Sam while Simon Pegg voices Bob the cat. How does their comedic banter anchor the emotional heart of the film?
★ What makes a buddy-comedy pairing between two opposite characters so fun to watch?

The animation features elaborate physical slapstick, like Sam getting tangled in tape or catching falling keys. How difficult is timing in digital animation?
★ Why is physical comedy so effective across different cultures and age groups?

The film incorporates global superstitions : black cats, four-leaf clovers, pennies, horseshoe arches, and staircases. How does tapping into folklore engage viewers?
★ What is a common superstition from your home culture, and do you secretly believe in it?

Babe the Dragon, voiced by Jane Fonda, combines majestic elegance with maternal warmth. How does voice casting shape character presence?
★ How does a veteran actor's voice bring authority and grace to an animated character?

The narrative explores the foster care system with gentleness, highlighting the bond between Sam and Hazel. How sensitive is the storytelling (e.g., examining light, framing, or pacing choices)?
★ Why is it important for animated movies to tackle real-world topics like adoption and foster care?

The climax shows Sam crafting a new balanced coin made from equal parts Good Luck and Bad Luck dust. How powerful is this visual metaphor?
★ Why is balance a healthier goal in life than striving for complete perfection?

The musical score by John Debney blends Celtic folk instruments with modern pop rhythms. How does music reinforce the leprechaun aesthetic?
★ How can traditional folk instruments give a fantasy film a unique geographic identity?

Luck was produced by Skydance Animation as their debut feature film. How does its visual polish compare to established animation studios?
★ What qualities do you look for when watching a new animation studio's inaugural feature film?

If you could design your own magical realm responsible for a human emotion or experience, what concept would your world manufacture?
★ What human experience (such as dreams, inspiration, or laughter) would you turn into an animated world?

ul.li: Incorrect: I will resign if they skimp always on budget → Correct: I will resign if they always skimp on budget (Frequency adverbs like 'always' come before the main verb.)
Incorrect: We are living here since two years → Correct: We have been living here for two years (Use present perfect continuous with 'for' to express duration.)
Incorrect: They don't allow her leave the house → Correct: They don't allow her to leave the house (Use 'allow someone to do something' construction.)
